findings.title: Denial cache key can collide across different resources (underscore delimiter)
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user UID, action, resource name and parent folder with `_` as the only separator. Resource names and folder UIDs in Grafana may legally contain underscores, so distinct checks produce identical keys, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") both yield `...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. Because `Check` now returns an immediate deny on a key hit (service.go:117), a legitimate deny for one resource will spuriously deny access to a different resource for the whole 30s TTL, with no way for the caller to recover. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in UIDs, or hash/length-prefix the components.

findings.title: Denial is cached even when the deny came from a stale folder tree, stacking staleness
findings.body: When the cached permissions do not grant access, the code re-queries permissions from the DB, but `checkInheritedPermissions`/`buildFolderTree` still use the 30s-cached folder tree (service.go:609-635). If the folder tree is stale and does not yet contain a freshly created parent folder, the check denies and that deny is then stored in `permDenialCache` for another full TTL. The staleness windows add up (up to ~2x shortCacheTTL), so a user who just created a nested folder/dashboard can keep being denied even after the permission refresh - exactly the scenario this PR aims to fix. Either bypass/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path, or do not cache denials that were produced by an inherited-permission lookup against a cached tree.

findings.title: Every non-granting cached check now triggers a full DB permission re-query
findings.body: `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` no longer short-circuit on the permission cache (the cache lookups were removed), and `Check` only returns early when the cached permissions grant access. Consequently every Check for a resource the user is not (yet) known to have access to performs the full store path again (basic role, teams, `GetUserPermissions`) instead of being served from the 30s cache. The denial cache only bounds this per (action, name, folder) tuple, so workloads that check many distinct objects (e.g. per-item authorization over a large dashboard set) will issue one permission query per object per TTL, a large increase in DB load compared to the previous behaviour. Consider limiting the DB fallback (e.g. only when the cached entry is older than a short grace period, or once per user/action per interval).

findings.title: Denial cache has unbounded key cardinality (one entry per user/action/name/folder)
findings.body: The denial cache key includes the requested resource name and parent folder, so the number of entries grows with the number of distinct objects ever denied, per user and action. With a local in-memory cache that has no size limit (see `cache.NewLocalCache` in pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:88), a user or service scanning many resources they cannot access (thousands of dashboards) will populate thousands of entries within each 30s window, which can translate into significant memory pressure on large instances. A bounded/LRU cache or a coarser key is needed.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric is now misleading
findings.body: `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" on a denial-cache hit (line 118), mixing two different caches into one hit-rate metric, and it is incremented with "false" at line 137 even when the permission cache was actually hit but simply did not grant access. The resulting cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts for the permission cache will report wrong values. Use a separate label/metric for the denial cache and only report "false" on a real permission-cache miss.

findings.title: Denial key uses raw subject UID while permission key uses resolved UID
findings.body: The denial key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject identifier from the request), whereas `userPermCacheKey` is built from `userIdentifiers.UID` resolved via `GetUserIdentifiers` (which treats numeric subjects as internal IDs). For a subject passed as `user:<numeric id>` the two caches are keyed on different identifiers, so the same user gets duplicate/independent denial entries depending on the subject form used by the caller, and denial entries cannot be reasoned about together with the permission entries. Resolve identifiers first and key both caches on the same resolved UID.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually exercise the short-circuit and its comment is wrong
findings.body: In "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but the permission cache is seeded with `{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. not allowed. Additionally `s.store`/`s.permissionStore` are the default empty `fakeStore`, which returns no permissions. The assertion `resp.Allowed == false` therefore holds even if the denial cache were ignored entirely, so the test gives no coverage of the new early-return path. Seed the permission cache with `true` (and/or a store that grants access) so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted.
